rules.title: Read the Approach First
rules.shortGuidance: Predictive, Agile, or Hybrid? The approach decides the answer.
rules.description: Applies before every other rule. Identify how the project is being delivered, because the same situation has different correct answers in each approach. Predictive signals: baseline, WBS, change control board, integrated change control, project management plan, phase gate. Agile signals: sprint, iteration, backlog, product owner, daily standup, increment, Kanban, retrospective. Hybrid wraps predictive governance around iterative delivery, so the governance rules apply to the wrapper and the Agile rules apply to the delivery. When a question names an artifact or a ceremony, it is telling you the approach on purpose.
rules.pmiPattern: Spot the signals · Name the approach · Then choose the rule

rules.title: Investigate Before Acting
rules.shortGuidance: Understand the cause first, unless something is going wrong right now.
rules.description: Applies to almost every question that asks what the project manager should do first. Gather the facts, assess the impact, and find the root cause before selecting a solution. Analyze, verify, and talk to the person closest to the work rather than reacting to a surface symptom. The exception matters as much as the rule: when there is an active safety hazard, a security or data breach, or live legal exposure, contain it first and investigate afterward. Protective action beats analysis only when harm is already in progress, not when harm is merely possible.
rules.pmiPattern: Contain real harm · Otherwise analyze · Find root cause · Then act

rules.title: Go to the Source
rules.shortGuidance: Talk to the people doing the work before you talk about them.
rules.description: Applies when a team member, stakeholder, or communication problem appears. The team members are the experts, not the project manager. When performance drops, an estimate slips, or a conflict surfaces, the first move is a direct conversation with the people involved, not a report, not a tool, and not their manager. Serve the team: remove obstacles and coach capability instead of issuing instructions, and never solve a people problem by reaching for a process. When nobody on the team knows, bring in a subject matter expert or check the lessons learned register rather than guessing.
rules.pmiPattern: Ask the person · Listen · Coach · Remove the obstacle · Then decide

rules.title: Know Who Owns the Decision
rules.shortGuidance: Solve it at your level. Escalate only to the person who owns it.
rules.description: Applies when a decision, conflict, or approval is in question. Ownership, not seniority, decides where a call belongs. The product owner owns scope, priority, and acceptance. The sponsor owns the budget and the business case. The change control board owns baseline changes. The functional or resource manager owns staffing. The project manager owns everything else and is expected to resolve it directly. Escalate only when the PM genuinely lacks the authority, an ethics or compliance line is at risk, a documented tolerance has actually been crossed, specialist expertise is required, or direct resolution has been attempted and failed. Escalating early looks weak, and escalating over someone else's decision right is worse.
rules.pmiPattern: Identify the owner · Attempt direct resolution · Then escalate

rules.title: Change Follows the Baseline
rules.shortGuidance: Baselined work needs change control. Backlog work needs a conversation.
rules.description: Applies when any modification to scope, schedule, cost, quality, or process is requested. In Predictive delivery every change, including a small or clearly beneficial one, is documented, assessed for impact across scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk, submitted through integrated change control, approved, and only then implemented with the baselines updated. In Agile delivery there is no change request. New or changed requirements go to the product owner, who orders them into the backlog for a future iteration while the current iteration stays protected. In Hybrid, ask which side of the line the change sits on: contract, budget, and milestone commitments go through governance, and delivery detail goes to the backlog.
rules.pmiPattern: Assess impact · Predictive: approve, then rebaseline · Agile: reprioritize the backlog

rules.title: Value Sets the Sequence
rules.shortGuidance: Deliver benefit early. When time is tight, cut by value, never by quality.
rules.description: Applies when work must be prioritized, sequenced, or traded off. Order the work by business value, benefit, and strategic alignment rather than by ease or preference. Prove assumptions with a minimum viable product, a prototype, or a demo before building at scale, and get feedback from the actual customer rather than a proxy. When schedule pressure arrives, understand what is driving it before reaching for crashing or fast tracking. If something has to give, reduce or defer the lowest value scope with the owner's agreement and in the open. Quality and compliance are never the release valve, and scope is never cut quietly.
rules.pmiPattern: Rank by value · Prove it small · Trade scope openly · Never trade quality

rules.title: Read the Metric, Then Its Limits
rules.shortGuidance: Numbers narrow the question. They rarely answer it on their own.
rules.description: Applies when a question turns on a metric, variance, forecast, or schedule calculation. Know what each measure actually says. CPI below 1.0 means a cost overrun and says nothing about schedule, while SPI drifts back toward 1.0 as a late project finishes no matter how late it is. EAC and VAC forecast the outcome, and TCPI states the efficiency still required to hit the target. Total float is schedule flexibility rather than spare time to spend, and only the critical path drives the finish date. Velocity, burndown, and cycle time describe one team's own trend and are never used to compare two teams. Read the number, say what it cannot tell you, then find the cause behind it before recommending anything.
rules.pmiPattern: Read the metric · Name its blind spot · Find the cause · Then recommend

rules.title: When Rules Collide, Follow the Ladder
rules.shortGuidance: Safety and compliance first, preference last. Never trade down the ladder.
rules.description: Applies whenever two rules both seem right, which is what most hard questions are testing. The order is: safety, ethics, and legal or regulatory compliance first, because these are boundaries rather than trade-offs and no schedule, cost, sponsor pressure, or customer request outranks them. Then decision rights and governance. Then stakeholder alignment and transparency. Then value. Then schedule and cost. Personal or organizational preference comes last and never beats anything above it. If an option asks you to conceal, defer, or quietly work around a compliance obligation, it is wrong no matter how sensible it sounds commercially.
rules.pmiPattern: Compliance · Decision rights · Alignment · Value · Schedule · Preference

glossary.definition: The person responsible for leading the project team and delivering project objectives within constraints.
glossary.why: The PM facilitates, communicates, and coordinates, but does not own technical decisions or personnel evaluations in matrix organizations.
glossary.trap: Assuming the PM has authority over everything. In matrix orgs, the Functional Manager owns personnel. The PM owns the work.

glossary.definition: The Agile role responsible for maximizing product value by owning and prioritizing the product backlog.
glossary.why: The Product Owner decides what gets built and in what order. No one else owns this.
glossary.trap: Thinking the Scrum Master or PM prioritizes the backlog. That is the Product Owner's exclusive responsibility.

glossary.definition: A servant leader who facilitates Agile ceremonies, removes impediments, and helps the team improve.
glossary.why: The Scrum Master coaches rather than directs. They do not assign tasks or make product decisions.
glossary.trap: Confusing the Scrum Master with a project manager. The Scrum Master serves the team. They do not manage it.

glossary.definition: The executive who provides funding, strategic direction, and business justification for the project.
glossary.why: The Sponsor owns the business case and makes continuation or termination decisions. Major issues escalate to the Sponsor after the PM has exhausted resolution options.
glossary.trap: Escalating to the Sponsor too early. PMI expects the PM to resolve issues at the lowest appropriate level first.

glossary.definition: Any individual, group, or organization that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself affected by a project decision.
glossary.why: Stakeholders must be identified, analyzed, and engaged throughout the project, not just at initiation.
glossary.trap: Treating stakeholder identification as a one-time activity. Stakeholder influence and interest can change throughout the project.

glossary.definition: A manager who owns a department or function and controls the people assigned to work on projects.
glossary.why: In matrix organizations, Functional Managers own staffing decisions and formal performance evaluations. The PM does not.
glossary.trap: Assuming the PM can direct personnel actions in a matrix org. Resource and HR authority belongs to the Functional Manager.

glossary.definition: An individual contributor who performs project work and delivers project outputs.
glossary.why: PMI favors empowering team members to self-organize and make decisions within their domain rather than directing every action.
glossary.trap: Treating team members as task executors. PMI values collaborative ownership and coaching over directive management.

glossary.definition: The individual or organization that will use or benefit from the project's deliverables.
glossary.why: Customer satisfaction and value delivery are central to PMI's definition of project success.
glossary.trap: Confusing the customer with the end user. The customer may commission the work while end users are different people.

glossary.definition: A governance body that provides oversight, strategic direction, and major decision authority for a project or program.
glossary.why: The Steering Committee escalation path is reserved for decisions that exceed the PM's authority.
glossary.trap: Escalating to the Steering Committee before attempting resolution at lower levels.

glossary.definition: The Project Management Office. A group that standardizes project governance, provides templates, and may oversee portfolio decisions.
glossary.why: PMOs support organizational project management maturity. Their authority varies by organization.
glossary.trap: Assuming all PMOs have the same authority. Some are supportive, some controlling, some directive.

glossary.definition: A practitioner who guides teams and organizations through Agile adoption and improvement.
glossary.why: Agile Coaches focus on cultural and process transformation, not day-to-day task management.
glossary.trap: Confusing the Agile Coach with the Scrum Master. Coaches operate at the team and organizational level; Scrum Masters are team-specific.

glossary.definition: A practitioner who elicits, documents, and validates requirements between business stakeholders and the project team.
glossary.why: Business Analysts bridge communication between stakeholders and technical teams. Requirements quality directly affects project outcomes.
glossary.trap: Assuming requirements are complete after the BA documents them. Requirements should be traced and validated throughout execution.

glossary.definition: An external organization contracted to provide goods, services, or results to the project.
glossary.why: Vendor relationships are governed by contracts. PMI expects decisions to follow contractual obligations, not relationship preferences.
glossary.trap: Approving extra vendor work or payment outside contract terms to preserve the relationship. Contract terms govern.

glossary.definition: A role responsible for a product's overall strategy, roadmap, and market success. Typically broader than the Product Owner.
glossary.why: Product Managers think across releases and market cycles. Product Owners focus on sprint-level backlog execution.
glossary.trap: Using Product Owner and Product Manager interchangeably. They have distinct scopes of responsibility.

glossary.definition: The document that formally authorizes a project, names the Project Manager, and establishes high-level objectives.
glossary.why: The Project Charter is the foundation of project authority. Without it, the PM has no formal standing.
glossary.trap: Treating the charter as interchangeable with the Project Management Plan. The charter authorizes; the plan defines how.

glossary.definition: The master document describing how the project will be executed, monitored, and controlled.
glossary.why: The Project Management Plan is the baseline for all decisions. Changes must go through change control.
glossary.trap: Treating the PM Plan as static. It is a living document updated through approved change requests.

glossary.definition: The document justifying the investment in a project based on expected benefits, costs, and strategic alignment.
glossary.why: The Business Case should be validated throughout the project, not just at initiation. Changing conditions may invalidate assumptions.
glossary.trap: Assuming the Business Case is only relevant at project start. PMI expects ongoing reassessment of value.

glossary.definition: A document that identifies stakeholders and records their interests, influence, engagement levels, and communication needs.
glossary.why: Stakeholder analysis is iterative. The register should be updated as stakeholder roles and influence change.
glossary.trap: Treating the Stakeholder Register as complete after initiation. It must evolve throughout the project.

glossary.definition: The document that records identified risks, their analysis, owners, and planned response strategies.
glossary.why: Risks are managed through the Risk Register. When triggers occur, planned responses should be executed first.
glossary.trap: Documenting active issues in the Risk Register. Issues belong in the Issue Log. Risks are future uncertainties.

glossary.definition: A document that records active problems currently affecting the project.
glossary.why: Issues require active management and ownership. They are distinct from risks because they have already occurred.
glossary.trap: Confusing risks with issues. A risk is uncertain and future; an issue is certain and present.

glossary.definition: A consolidated tracking tool that captures Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies in one place, each with an owner and a status.
glossary.why: A RAID Log gives one visible home for open items and their owners - useful during delivery and especially at closure, when unfinished work, decisions, and handoffs must be tracked and transferred so nothing is lost.
glossary.trap: Reaching for the RAID Log when a question names a specific artifact. A realized problem still belongs in the Issue Log, and a future uncertainty in the Risk Register.

glossary.definition: A record of knowledge gained during the project that can improve future performance.
glossary.why: Lessons learned are most valuable when captured and shared proactively, not just archived at closure.
glossary.trap: Treating lessons learned as an end-of-project formality. They should be captured and applied throughout.

glossary.definition: A record of all change requests submitted, their status, and final disposition.
glossary.why: The Change Log provides traceability for all scope, schedule, cost, and quality changes.
glossary.trap: Confusing the Change Log with the Lessons Learned Register. Change Log tracks decisions; Lessons Learned captures knowledge.

glossary.definition: A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable, baseline, or process.
glossary.why: Every change, even a small one, should be evaluated through change control. Bypassing the process creates uncontrolled scope.
glossary.trap: Implementing small changes without a change request because they seem minor. Cumulative minor changes can significantly affect the project.

glossary.definition: The prioritized list of all work needed for the product, owned and managed by the Product Owner.
glossary.why: The Product Backlog is the single source of work for an Agile team. Only the Product Owner decides priority.
glossary.trap: Allowing stakeholders to add items directly to the backlog without Product Owner review and prioritization.

glossary.definition: The subset of Product Backlog items selected for a sprint, owned by the development team.
glossary.why: The Sprint Backlog represents the team's commitment for the sprint. External parties should not add to it mid-sprint.
glossary.trap: Allowing managers or stakeholders to add work to the Sprint Backlog after sprint planning.

glossary.definition: A document that establishes team working agreements, ground rules, responsibilities, and expectations.
glossary.why: Team Charters prevent confusion and conflict by establishing shared expectations upfront.
glossary.trap: Skipping the team charter to start work faster. Unclear expectations create more disruption than the time saved.

glossary.definition: A document that describes expected benefits, how they will be measured, and who owns them after delivery.
glossary.why: PMI distinguishes between delivering outputs and realizing benefits. The Benefits Management Plan bridges that gap.
glossary.trap: Assuming deliverable acceptance equals benefits realization. Benefits must be measured after implementation.

glossary.definition: A document defining what information each stakeholder needs, when, how, and from whom.
glossary.why: Effective communication is tailored to stakeholder needs, not the same format for everyone.
glossary.trap: Sending the same report to all stakeholders. Effective communication requires tailoring by audience.

glossary.definition: Work Breakdown Structure. A hierarchical decomposition of total project work into manageable components.
glossary.why: The WBS defines the scope baseline. Everything in the WBS is in scope; everything outside it is not.
glossary.trap: Including activities or processes in the WBS. The WBS contains deliverables, not actions.

glossary.definition: A grid linking requirements to their source, status, and associated deliverables throughout the project.
glossary.why: Traceability ensures requirements are not lost and are validated through testing.
glossary.trap: Skipping traceability because requirements seem stable. Untraceable requirements create gaps during testing.

glossary.definition: A fixed time box (usually 1 to 4 weeks) during which the Scrum Team delivers a potentially shippable increment.
glossary.why: Sprint scope is committed by the team. External requests should not interrupt sprint commitments.
glossary.trap: Adding work mid-sprint because a stakeholder requests it urgently. New requests go to the Product Backlog.

glossary.definition: The ceremony where the team selects backlog items and plans how to complete them in the upcoming sprint.
glossary.why: The Scrum Team commits to sprint work. The PM, Sponsor, and stakeholders do not.
glossary.trap: Allowing outside parties to dictate sprint scope. Only the team can commit to what they will deliver.

glossary.definition: The ceremony where the team demonstrates the increment to stakeholders and collects feedback.
glossary.why: New requests from Sprint Reviews should be added to the Product Backlog for prioritization, not implemented immediately.
glossary.trap: Beginning implementation of Sprint Review requests right away. All requests must be evaluated and prioritized first.

glossary.definition: The ceremony where the team reflects on their process and identifies improvements for the next sprint.
glossary.why: Retrospective improvement actions should be tracked and followed through, not just identified.
glossary.trap: Identifying improvements but never implementing them. Retrospectives only add value when action items are executed.

glossary.definition: The ongoing process of reviewing, clarifying, estimating, and ordering backlog items.
glossary.why: Refinement ensures work is clear and ready for sprint planning. Ambiguous items should be refined before commitment.
glossary.trap: Starting sprint planning with unrefined items. Unclear stories create planning instability and rework.

glossary.definition: A shared agreement on the criteria that must be met for work to be considered complete.
glossary.why: Meeting the Definition of Done means the increment is potentially shippable, but that does not automatically mean it should be released.
glossary.trap: Assuming that meeting the Definition of Done triggers an automatic release. Release is a separate Product Owner decision.

glossary.definition: The amount of work a team completes per sprint, used for planning and forecasting.
glossary.why: Velocity changes should be analyzed before corrective action is selected. Declining velocity has many possible causes.
glossary.trap: Immediately adding resources when velocity drops. The cause must be understood before the response is selected.

glossary.definition: A short description of a feature from the user's perspective, typically in the format: As a [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit].
glossary.why: User stories focus on value from the user's perspective. They should be small enough to complete within a sprint.
glossary.trap: Writing user stories too large to estimate or complete. Stories that span multiple sprints should be split.

glossary.definition: Criteria that must be met before a backlog item can be pulled into a sprint.
glossary.why: Ready items prevent ambiguity from entering the sprint and disrupting team commitments.
glossary.trap: Confusing Definition of Ready with Definition of Done. Ready = entry criteria; Done = exit criteria.

glossary.definition: A leadership philosophy where the leader's primary role is to support, enable, and develop the team.
glossary.why: PMI increasingly favors servant leadership over directive management. The leader removes obstacles rather than directing every action.
glossary.trap: Solving problems for the team instead of helping the team solve them. Servant leadership builds capability, not dependency.

glossary.definition: The process of reviewing, evaluating, approving, or rejecting all change requests across all project components.
glossary.why: Every change, regardless of size, must be evaluated through integrated change control to prevent uncontrolled scope growth.
glossary.trap: Bypassing change control for small or "obvious" changes. Even beneficial changes require impact assessment.

glossary.definition: A group with authority to approve or reject change requests.
glossary.why: CCB approval is required before implementing changes that affect project baselines.
glossary.trap: Implementing changes before CCB approval because they seem low risk or have stakeholder support.

glossary.definition: The approved version of scope, schedule, or cost against which project performance is measured.
glossary.why: Baselines can only be changed through formal change control. Unauthorized changes invalidate performance measurements.
glossary.trap: Updating baselines informally to match current state. Baselines require approved change requests.

glossary.definition: Unauthorized expansion of project scope without corresponding adjustments to time, cost, or resources.
glossary.why: Scope creep is one of the leading causes of project failure. Even small unauthorized additions accumulate.
glossary.trap: Allowing minor uncontrolled additions because they seem harmless. Cumulative scope creep significantly impacts delivery.

glossary.definition: Adding features or functionality beyond what the customer requested.
glossary.why: Gold plating consumes resources, adds risk, and creates unverified scope, even when well-intentioned.
glossary.trap: Thinking customers will appreciate extra work. Gold plating creates risk without approved value.

glossary.definition: The process of identifying, tracking, and controlling project documents, deliverables, and product versions.
glossary.why: Configuration management ensures the right version of documents and deliverables is always in use.
glossary.trap: Treating configuration management as optional. Version confusion creates rework and scope disputes.

glossary.definition: An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, will have a positive or negative effect on project objectives.
glossary.why: Risk is future and uncertain. The appropriate response depends on probability, impact, and context.
glossary.trap: Treating every concern as a risk. Active problems are issues. Risks are still uncertain.

glossary.definition: A problem that has already occurred and requires active management.
glossary.why: Issues require different management than risks. Active problems belong in the Issue Log, not the Risk Register.
glossary.trap: Logging active problems in the Risk Register. Issues are certain; risks are uncertain.

glossary.definition: The planned action to address a risk: avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, or escalate.
glossary.why: When a risk trigger occurs, the planned response should be executed first, before creating new approaches or escalating.
glossary.trap: Creating new responses when triggers occur instead of implementing the approved plan.

glossary.definition: Budget or time set aside to address identified risks that occur.
glossary.why: Contingency reserves are for known risks. Management reserves are for unknown risks. They are not interchangeable.
glossary.trap: Using management reserves for identified risks. Contingency reserves exist for planned risk responses.

glossary.definition: Budget set aside for unknown risks, meaning events not identified during planning.
glossary.why: Management reserves require executive approval to access. They cannot be used without authorization.
glossary.trap: Treating management reserves as extra contingency for known risks.

glossary.definition: The remaining risk after a response strategy has been implemented.
glossary.why: Risk responses rarely eliminate risk entirely. Residual risks require ongoing monitoring.
glossary.trap: Closing a risk after a response is implemented without evaluating residual exposure.

glossary.definition: A new risk that arises as a direct result of implementing a risk response.
glossary.why: Risk responses can create new risks. These must be identified, documented, and managed.
glossary.trap: Closing a risk without checking whether the response created new risks.

glossary.definition: The degree of uncertainty an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives.
glossary.why: Risk responses and thresholds should align with organizational risk appetite.
glossary.trap: Making risk decisions without understanding organizational risk tolerance.

glossary.definition: The process of communicating with, influencing, and managing stakeholder expectations throughout the project.
glossary.why: Stakeholder engagement is proactive and continuous. It cannot be treated as periodic or one-directional.
glossary.trap: Assuming that distributing reports equals stakeholder engagement. True engagement involves dialogue and feedback.

glossary.definition: The process of addressing disagreements between stakeholders, team members, or other parties.
glossary.why: PMI expects the PM to attempt direct resolution before escalating. Collaboration and problem-solving are preferred over avoidance.
glossary.trap: Escalating conflicts too early. Direct communication and collaboration should be the first response.

glossary.definition: The act of raising a problem, decision, or conflict to a higher authority for resolution.
glossary.why: Escalation is appropriate when the PM lacks authority, ethics or compliance are involved, or direct resolution has failed.
glossary.trap: Escalating before attempting direct resolution. PMI expects issues to be resolved at the lowest appropriate level first.

glossary.definition: The process of guiding a group toward a productive outcome or decision.
glossary.why: Facilitation is a core PM competency for alignment sessions, retrospectives, and conflict resolution.
glossary.trap: Confusing facilitation with decision-making. The facilitator guides the process; the group makes the decision.

glossary.definition: A communication technique involving full attention, clarifying questions, and confirming understanding.
glossary.why: Active listening improves stakeholder engagement and reduces miscommunication.
glossary.trap: Assuming understanding without confirming. Active listening requires verification of what was heard.

glossary.definition: Process-focused activities that ensure quality standards are being applied consistently.
glossary.why: QA is proactive and process-oriented. It happens during execution to prevent defects.
glossary.trap: Confusing QA with QC. QA audits the process; QC inspects the product.

glossary.definition: Product-focused activities that inspect outputs to identify defects.
glossary.why: QC is reactive and product-oriented. It happens after work is done to find problems.
glossary.trap: Relying only on QC. Prevention is less costly than inspection.

glossary.definition: A systematic process for identifying the underlying cause of a problem.
glossary.why: PMI favors addressing root causes over treating symptoms. Corrective actions should follow analysis.
glossary.trap: Implementing solutions before identifying the root cause. This produces recurring problems.

glossary.definition: The total cost of ensuring quality, including prevention, appraisal, and failure costs.
glossary.why: Prevention costs less than failure. Investing in quality upfront reduces total project cost.
glossary.trap: Treating quality investment as overhead. The cost of poor quality (rework, defects) typically exceeds prevention costs.

glossary.definition: An ongoing effort to improve products, processes, or services over time.
glossary.why: Continuous improvement is embedded in Agile through retrospectives and in predictive projects through lessons learned.
glossary.trap: Identifying improvements without implementing them. Improvement only happens when actions are completed.

glossary.definition: Cost Performance Index. EV ÷ AC. Above 1.0 means under budget; below 1.0 means over budget.
glossary.why: CPI measures cost efficiency. A poor CPI requires investigation and corrective action, not immediate scope changes.
glossary.trap: Ignoring CPI when SPI looks good. Both metrics must be evaluated together.

glossary.definition: Schedule Performance Index. EV ÷ PV. Above 1.0 means ahead of schedule; below 1.0 means behind.
glossary.why: SPI identifies schedule variance but not the cause. Analysis is required before selecting a response.
glossary.trap: Adding resources when SPI is low without understanding why. Not all schedule delays are resource-solvable.

glossary.definition: Earned Value. The budgeted value of work actually completed.
glossary.why: EV is the foundation of earned value analysis. It measures what was accomplished, not what was spent.
glossary.trap: Confusing EV with AC. EV is the value of work done; AC is what was spent to do it.

glossary.definition: The process of determining the cause and magnitude of cost and schedule differences from the plan.
glossary.why: Variance analysis must precede corrective action. Selecting a response before knowing the cause is a common PMI trap.
glossary.trap: Acting on variance without analysis. The corrective action depends entirely on the cause of the variance.

glossary.definition: Predicting future project performance based on current status and historical trends.
glossary.why: Forecasts should be validated, especially AI-generated ones, before driving decisions.
glossary.trap: Treating forecasts as facts. Forecasts are estimates and should be validated against current conditions.

glossary.definition: The process of ensuring that expected benefits are actually achieved after the project delivers its outputs.
glossary.why: PMI distinguishes between delivering outputs and realizing benefits. A project can meet all technical objectives and still fail to deliver value.
glossary.trap: Assuming deliverable acceptance means benefits are realized. Benefits require measurement, ownership, and time.

glossary.definition: The degree to which a project supports the organization's current strategic objectives.
glossary.why: Projects should be periodically reassessed against organizational strategy, especially when business conditions change.
glossary.trap: Assuming strategic alignment at initiation is permanent. Market, organizational, or competitive changes can shift alignment.

glossary.definition: The net benefit an organization receives from a project, including financial, customer, operational, and strategic outcomes.
glossary.why: PMI's definition of value is broad. Schedule and budget performance alone do not define business value.
glossary.trap: Equating on-time, on-budget delivery with value. A project can meet all delivery metrics and still fail to create value.

glossary.definition: Output = what was built. Outcome = the change in behavior, capability, or value that the output enables.
glossary.why: PMI increasingly measures success by outcomes, not just outputs. A delivered product that isn't adopted produces no outcome.
glossary.trap: Celebrating delivery without measuring adoption or business impact. Outputs are necessary but not sufficient.

glossary.definition: A symptom is the visible sign of a problem. A root cause is the underlying reason the problem exists.
glossary.why: PMI always favors fixing root causes over treating symptoms. Symptom-based solutions produce recurring problems.
glossary.trap: Acting on the visible problem without investigating its source. The right solution depends on the real cause.

glossary.definition: Escalation passes a problem to a higher authority. Resolution addresses it at the current level.
glossary.why: PMI expects the PM to resolve issues at the lowest appropriate level. Escalation is appropriate only when authority, ethics, or compliance require it.
glossary.trap: Escalating too early to avoid discomfort. PMI views premature escalation as failure to own the problem.

glossary.definition: The first action is what to do immediately given current information. The final action is the ultimate resolution.
glossary.why: Most PMP exam questions ask for the FIRST action, which is almost always to investigate, verify, or align before acting.
glossary.trap: Selecting the correct final action rather than the correct first action. PMI rewards gathering information and aligning before deciding.

glossary.definition: Analysis means understanding the situation. Action means doing something about it.
glossary.why: PMI consistently rewards analysis before action. Acting without analysis produces misaligned solutions.
glossary.trap: Selecting an action answer when the question asks what to do first. Analysis almost always precedes action in PMI reasoning.

glossary.definition: Validation confirms that a recommendation, plan, or output is correct or appropriate. Implementation executes it.
glossary.why: PMI requires validation, especially of AI-generated recommendations, before implementation.
glossary.trap: Implementing AI recommendations or stakeholder requests without validation. All recommendations should be verified against project context.

glossary.definition: Governance ensures process compliance. Value delivery ensures the right outcomes are achieved.
glossary.why: PMI increasingly emphasizes value alongside governance. Process compliance does not guarantee value.
glossary.trap: Assuming that following the process guarantees success. Governance and value are both necessary.

glossary.definition: Collaboration means working together toward a shared solution. Directive action means one party imposing a decision.
glossary.why: PMI favors collaboration before directive action, especially in conflict situations and stakeholder disagreements.
glossary.trap: Imposing a decision to resolve a conflict quickly. PMI prefers facilitating shared understanding first.

glossary.definition: Using AI tools to generate recommendations, forecasts, or analyses that inform project decisions.
glossary.why: AI outputs must be validated before acting on them. AI supplements human judgment. It does not replace it.
glossary.trap: Implementing AI recommendations without validating assumptions. AI tools can produce plausible but incorrect outputs.

glossary.definition: The degree to which end users and operational teams are prepared to successfully use a delivered solution.
glossary.why: Technical completion without adoption readiness produces no benefits. User confusion reduces realized value.
glossary.trap: Releasing because the Definition of Done is met without assessing whether users can successfully adopt the solution.

glossary.definition: The state of being prepared to operate and support a delivered solution on an ongoing basis.
glossary.why: PMI expects benefits to be sustained after delivery. Operational teams must be ready to support and maintain what was built.
glossary.trap: Closing a project before operational teams have the knowledge and support needed to sustain benefits.

glossary.definition: The process of ensuring relevant project knowledge reaches those who need it, especially operational teams.
glossary.why: Without effective knowledge transfer, benefits erode over time as project team members move on.
glossary.trap: Treating documentation as sufficient knowledge transfer. Real transfer requires engagement, not just files.

glossary.definition: Value that persists and grows after the project closes, rather than eroding due to operational complexity or cost.
glossary.why: PMI evaluates value holistically, including long-term costs, maintenance burden, and organizational impact.
glossary.trap: Optimizing for short-term customer satisfaction without considering long-term operational sustainability.

glossary.definition: The right and responsibility to make a specific type of decision within a project or organization.
glossary.why: PMI exam questions frequently test whether candidates know who owns which decision. Role clarity prevents confusion and conflicts.
glossary.trap: Assuming the PM has decision authority over everything. Authority varies by organization structure and decision type.

glossary.definition: The process of bringing new stakeholders up to speed on project objectives, decisions, and governance.
glossary.why: New stakeholders who lack context create recurring confusion and conflict. Proactive onboarding prevents systemic engagement problems.
glossary.trap: Correcting stakeholder misunderstandings reactively. A structured onboarding approach is more effective.

glossary.definition: Giving the team authority, ownership, and autonomy to make decisions within their domain.
glossary.why: Empowered teams produce better outcomes and develop capability. PMI favors coaching and enabling over controlling.
glossary.trap: Removing autonomy to improve predictability. Directive management may appear faster but reduces team development and ownership.

questions.questionText: On a hybrid effort, the agile track considers work finished when it meets the team's definition of done, while the predictive track uses formal exit criteria. Integrated deliverables are being called complete by one standard but not the other, causing rework. What should the project manager do?
options: Reconcile the definition of done and exit criteria into one completion standard for integrated work.
Apply the predictive exit criteria to all integrated deliverables for consistency.
Have each track keep its own standard and check integrated work against both.
Adopt the agile definition of done across both tracks to simplify completion.
questions.explanation: The rework comes from two different definitions of complete colliding where the tracks integrate. Reconciling the definition of done and the exit criteria into one standard for integrated work gives both tracks a shared, unambiguous bar. Governing PMI principle: Establish a single, shared completion standard for integrated work.
questions.keyTakeaway: Where tracks integrate, agree one completion standard rather than imposing one side's or maintaining both.

questions.questionText: Jenna's retail project mixes office-based employees with fully remote contributors. The remote members report that key discussions and decisions keep happening in hallway conversations and impromptu desk huddles they are never part of, and they often learn outcomes after the fact. What is the underlying issue?
options: The remote members need better collaboration tools
The team has uneven access to information and decision-making
The remote members are not engaging enough with the team
The time-zone differences are too wide to coordinate
questions.explanation: Decisions forming in in-person side conversations create unequal access for remote members, which is the core equity issue. Tooling, remote engagement, and time zones are plausible reads but not what the scenario describes. Governing PMI principle: Stakeholders (ensure equitable access to information and decisions).
questions.keyTakeaway: Hybrid teams fail on equity when decisions form in in-person side channels.

questions.questionText: A new workstream is starting, and the organization's standard is to run everything predictively. The workstream's requirements are uncertain and likely to evolve as early prototypes get feedback. The project manager is deciding how to run it. What should the project manager do?
options: Choose the approach by weighing the workstream's requirement stability and risk.
Run the workstream predictively to stay consistent with the organization's standard.
Run the workstream with an agile approach to accommodate the evolving requirements.
Start the workstream predictively and switch to agile if the requirements prove unstable.
questions.explanation: Selecting an approach is a deliberate decision that weighs the work's characteristics, not a reflex toward the default or a single signal. Choosing by assessing requirement stability, risk, and the other relevant factors produces a justified fit for this workstream. Governing PMI principle: Tailor the delivery approach deliberately to the work rather than defaulting or reacting.
questions.keyTakeaway: Tailoring is a deliberate, multi-factor choice, not a default and not a reflex to one variable.

questions.questionText: Lorraine's company voluntarily committed to sourcing a portion of its materials from certified sustainable suppliers. A project team identifies a lower-cost supplier that would improve short-term economics but does not support the commitment. How should the commitment be treated in the decision?
options: As a factor that applies only when financial results remain unchanged
As a preference that should yield whenever lower-cost alternatives exist
As a branding objective that sits outside project value decisions
As a consideration weighed against other strategic objectives
questions.explanation: The commitment is not a legal mandate, but it is also more than a preference. Because the organization chose it as part of its strategic direction, it should be considered alongside other organizational objectives when evaluating value. Governing PMI principle: Stewardship (voluntary commitments are weighed among strategic objectives).
questions.keyTakeaway: Voluntary sustainability commitments should be evaluated alongside other strategic objectives rather than ignored or treated as absolute.

questions.questionText: Virgil's software team identifies a future dependency that could delay a release if an external vendor misses a planned delivery date. No impact has occurred yet. Which project record should be updated?
options: Risk register
Issue log
Change log
Lessons learned register
questions.explanation: The situation represents a future uncertainty rather than a current problem and should be managed accordingly. Governing PMI principle: Uncertainty (a potential future problem is a risk).
questions.keyTakeaway: Future uncertainty belongs in a different process than active problems.

questions.questionText: Rhea's sponsor at Orchard Bank wants to commit funding for a whole multi-year program upfront. The work is genuinely uncertain and the direction could shift as the team learns. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Fund the program in increments tied to validated progress
Fund the full multi-year program upfront for commitment
Fund only the first phase and decide the rest informally later
Fund the whole program but freeze spending if problems appear
questions.explanation: Uncertain work is best funded incrementally, releasing money against validated progress so investment follows what is learned rather than betting it all on an uncertain plan. Governing PMI principle: Value (fund incrementally against validated progress).
questions.keyTakeaway: Fund uncertain work incrementally against validated progress rather than committing it all upfront.

questions.questionText: A community group raises a concern that a project's planned work could negatively affect the local area. The project is permitted and within its rights to proceed. What should the project manager do?
options: Proceed with the work as planned, since the project already holds all the necessary permissions.
Refer the community group to the organization's public relations team.
Pause all the work until the community's concern is fully resolved.
Assess and address the community impact as part of delivering responsibly.
questions.explanation: Having permission to proceed does not settle whether the work affects the community in ways that should be addressed. Assessing the concern and addressing the impact treats the community as a legitimate consideration in delivering responsibly, beyond the minimum the permits require. Governing PMI principle: Deliver responsibly by considering the project's broader impact, not only its rights.
questions.keyTakeaway: Permission to proceed is not the whole question; assess and address community impact as part of responsible delivery.

questions.questionText: After a confirmed strategy change at Northwind Bank, the objectives, scope, and success measures of Sofia's project have all been informally adjusted, but the baseline still reflects the old strategy. The next steering review is months away. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Record the changes through change control without rebaselining
Rebaseline the project so it formally reflects the new strategy
Keep the old baseline as a historical reference and proceed
Leave the changes informal to preserve flexibility
questions.explanation: When objectives, scope, and measures have all shifted with a confirmed strategy change, the baseline must be reset to match; logging changes without rebaselining, keeping the old baseline, or staying informal all leave the project measured against a strategy it no longer follows. Governing PMI principle: Change (rebaseline after a confirmed change).
questions.keyTakeaway: After a confirmed strategy change reshapes objectives, scope, and measures, rebaseline so the project is governed against the new strategy.

questions.questionText: Errol's logistics project has completed several pilot deployments with positive operational results. Regional managers want immediate expansion, while support teams warn that training materials are still being refined. What is the most appropriate way to proceed?
options: Ask regional leaders to determine deployment timing.
Delay expansion until the core training is in place.
Expand deployment to capture early benefits.
Compare readiness factors to rollout objectives.
questions.explanation: Expansion decisions should consider both realized benefits and organizational readiness before rollout plans are adjusted. Governing PMI principle: Delivery (weigh readiness against rollout objectives).
questions.keyTakeaway: Scaling successful pilots requires balancing readiness with value realization.

questions.questionText: Wren leads a hybrid project at Fable Studios. The adaptive team wants to stop estimating altogether and simply flow work, but the predictive side needs forecast inputs to maintain the integrated plan. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Use lightweight forecasting to feed the plan, not detailed estimates
Require detailed estimates as the predictive plan has always used
Let the team stop estimating to respect their autonomy
Have the predictive side estimate the adaptive team's work for them
questions.explanation: The integrated plan needs forecast inputs, and the team has a fair point about wasted effort. Lightweight forecasting, such as throughput-based projection, feeds the plan while removing the low-value estimation the team objects to. Governing PMI principle: Tailoring (right-size estimation to what the plan needs).
questions.keyTakeaway: Keep the lightest forecasting the plan truly needs and drop estimation effort that adds no value.

questions.questionText: A sponsor at Riverstone Media verbally supports Hugo's strategic goals but has not committed the funding or decision authority the project needs to move, and work is about to stall. What should Hugo do next?
options: Proceed on the sponsor's verbal support
Keep planning and raise the commitment gap later
Escalate the sponsor's lack of commitment to senior leadership for resolution
Secure the committed funding and decision authority the project needs
questions.explanation: The project needs real commitment, so the next step is to secure the funding and authority from the sponsor; proceeding on words, escalating over the sponsor's head, or deferring the gap all leave the project without what it needs to move. Governing PMI principle: Stakeholders (secure committed funding and authority).
questions.keyTakeaway: Convert verbal support into committed funding and authority before proceeding, rather than relying on words or escalating prematurely.

questions.questionText: Jeff's telecommunications project has shipped three solid releases. Recently a senior engineer has gone quiet in planning, contributing only when work is assigned directly to them. Delivery metrics are still stable, but newer team members increasingly route every decision through that one engineer. Which action would most likely improve long-term team performance?
options: Create opportunities for shared technical leadership across the team
Move the engineer into a technical advisory role
Have the engineer mentor a couple of named successors on key decisions
Increase status-reporting requirements for the whole team
questions.explanation: The risk is over-dependence on one person, so distributing technical leadership builds the team's long-term capability. An advisory role or named-successor mentoring help narrowly; more status reporting addresses nothing about the dependency. Governing PMI principle: Team (distribute capability to reduce single-point dependence).
questions.keyTakeaway: Reduce single-point dependence by building shared leadership, not by formalizing the dependence.
